question: What is the primary financial goal of the Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: Providing free medications to all categories of hospital patients
options.B: Funding the construction of new hospital wards and theaters
options.C: Generating high profits for the hospital management
options.D: Sustaining a continuous supply of affordable essential medicines

explanation: The DRF aims to keep drugs available and affordable through a self-replenishing financial cycle rather than generating commercial profits. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h1)

question: How does the DRF maintain its operational capital over time?

options.A: By borrowing operational funds from commercial banks at low interest
options.B: By ploughing patient payments directly back into purchasing new drug stock
options.C: By charging high commercial markups on every prescription dispensed
options.D: Through monthly federal government subventions and foreign donor grants

explanation: The fund revolves because money collected from patients at the point of sale is reinvested immediately to buy replacement inventory. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h1)

question: Which practice directly violates core DRF management principles?

options.A: Keeping clear and transparent inventory record books
options.B: Reinvesting collected revenue into procuring replacement stock
options.C: Issuing drugs to patients on extended informal credit
options.D: Pricing medicines to cover basic replacement costs

explanation: Giving out drugs on credit breaks the revolving cycle by depriving the fund of the cash needed for immediate restocking. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h2)

question: Why is the separation of duties important in a DRF system?

options.A: It allows doctors to bypass pharmacists when prescribing emergency drugs
options.B: It speeds up the process of manufacturing generic medications locally
options.C: It ensures that nurses spend all their working hours on pharmacy duties
options.D: It prevents financial fraud and improves accountability among staff

explanation: Dividing responsibilities among different cadres ensures checks and balances, minimizing opportunities for theft and mismanagement. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h2)

question: What is a major frontline responsibility of the nurse in the DRF process?

options.A: Procuring bulk pharmaceutical supplies directly from overseas manufacturers
options.B: Administering prescribed DRF medications safely and minimizing wastage
options.C: Auditing the central hospital bank accounts at the end of every month
options.D: Setting the official retail prices for all medicines in the hospital

explanation: Nurses directly handle and administer drugs at the bedside, making safe administration and waste reduction their primary contribution. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h3)

question: A patient complains that DRF drugs are too expensive compared to roadside vendors. How should the nurse respond?

options.A: Explain that DRF drugs are genuine, safe, and priced to sustain availability
options.B: Advise the patient to buy from the roadside vendors to save money
options.C: Ignore the complaint because nurses are not responsible for drug prices
options.D: Pay for the patient's prescription out of personal pocket money

explanation: Nurses educate patients on the value of safety and quality assurance inherent in institutional DRF procurement. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h3)

question: What does the FIFO inventory rule require nurses to do?

options.A: File financial invoices in alphabetical order
options.B: Finish treating all emergency patients first
options.C: Use older stock items before newer supplies
options.D: Find identical items from five outside pharmacies

explanation: FIFO stands for First-In, First-Out, ensuring older inventory is utilized before newer stock to prevent expiration. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h4)

question: A nurse discovers a box of antibiotics expiring in two weeks inside the ward cupboard, while a newer box sits behind it. What action should the nurse take?

options.A: Send the expiring box back to the central store to be sold cheaply
options.B: Move the expiring box to the front and ensure it is dispensed first
options.C: Discard both boxes immediately to prevent any accidental medication errors
options.D: Leave the arrangement alone since all the antibiotics are the same drug

explanation: Applying FIFO principles prevents loss from expired stock by actively prioritizing older medications for immediate use. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h4)

question: Why is patient adherence education a vital part of the nurse's DRF responsibility?

options.A: It allows nurses to take over the role of the chief pharmacist
options.B: It replaces the need for doctors to write detailed case notes
options.C: It guarantees that the hospital pharmacy will make a large profit
options.D: It prevents treatment failure and reduces the waste of scarce drugs

explanation: When patients take medicines correctly, they recover faster, preventing complications and wasted pharmaceutical resources. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h5)

question: Which action represents rational drug administration by a nurse?

options.A: Giving leftover prescription drugs from one patient to another
options.B: Refusing to report mild skin rashes noticed after giving an injection
options.C: Administering drugs quickly without checking the patient identification band
options.D: Checking patient allergies and doses before administering medication

explanation: Patient safety protocols require verifying allergies and dosages to ensure appropriate and safe drug delivery. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is a recommended control measure against cash diversion in a DRF unit?

options.A: Issuing official receipts and using verified electronic payment channels
options.B: Stopping all cash transactions and offering drugs entirely on credit
options.C: Writing patient payments down on rough scratch paper
options.D: Allowing senior nurses to keep cash collections in their lockers

explanation: Official receipts and electronic audit trails protect revenue and maintain transparency within the revolving fund system. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h6)

question: Why is the practice of informal credit sales dangerous to the DRF?

options.A: It creates cash flow deficits that prevent timely restocking
options.B: It increases the physical workload of the nursing staff
options.C: It speeds up the rate at which ward shelves empty out
options.D: It forces pharmacists to order fake generic drugs from abroad

explanation: When money is owed informally and never repaid, the fund loses the liquid cash required to purchase new batch supplies. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h6)

question: How does severe inflation negatively affect a functional DRF system?

options.A: It reduces the purchasing power of the fund, making replacement stock harder to buy
options.B: It eliminates all forms of waste and pilferage in hospital wards
options.C: It makes patients need fewer medications during their clinic visits
options.D: It forces nurses to stop keeping physical stock inventory records

explanation: Inflation means replacement costs rise faster than expected, which can exhaust the revolving capital if prices are not adjusted appropriately. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h7)

question: Which strategy helps protect a DRF against total collapse during economic hardships?

options.A: Failing to review prices and selling drugs far below replacement cost
options.B: Implementing periodic realistic price adjustments and strong multidisciplinary oversight
options.C: Handing over all drug procurement tasks entirely to untrained volunteers
options.D: Stopping all financial audits to save time for clinical duties

explanation: Regular review of prices and active teamwork across departments help maintain fund solvency despite external economic pressures. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T7#GNS215_U3_T7_h7)
